hook: A coffee shop near campus drops its iced latte price from \$5 to \$4 for exam week, and the line runs out the door. A month later a new bubble tea shop opens next door, and the coffee shop sells fewer lattes at the same \$4. Both stories are about demand, but only one of them moves the demand curve.

prereq.q: Each extra slice of pizza you eat at a party satisfies you a little less than the one before. This is
options: a rise in total utility for each slice
prereq.why: Marginal utility, the extra satisfaction from one more unit, falls as you have more.

prereq.q: On a graph, a change that moves the whole curve to a new position is
options: a change in the slope only
a new point on the same curve
prereq.why: A shift moves the whole curve; a movement along it changes the point on the same curve.

prereq.q: A curve that slopes down from left to right shows
prereq.why: As one variable rises, the other falls.

figure.caption: Left: a lower price moves buyers along D from A to B. Right: higher incomes shift the whole curve from D1 to D2. Invented data for practice.

chain.cause: The price of a good falls, other things equal
chain.effect: the good is cheaper than its substitutes and buyers' money goes further

chain.cause: Buyers switch toward it and can afford more (the substitution and income effects)
The quantity demanded rises because of the good's own price
chain.effect: buyers move down along the same demand curve; the curve does not shift

ideas: Law of demand: other things equal, a higher price means a smaller quantity demanded. The curve slopes down.
It slopes down because of the substitution effect, the income effect and diminishing marginal utility.
A change in the good's own price is a movement along the curve: a change in quantity demanded.
A change in a determinant shifts the whole curve: tastes, income (normal or inferior), prices of substitutes and complements, expectations, the number of buyers.
Market demand is the horizontal sum of every buyer's quantity at each price.

misconception.wrong: When a good gets cheaper, its demand increases, so the demand curve shifts right.
misconception.right: A lower own price raises the quantity demanded: a movement down along the same curve. Demand shifts only when something other than the good's own price changes, such as income or the price of a related good.

summary: Demand shows how much buyers want at each price. By the law of demand, a higher price lowers the quantity demanded, because of the substitution and income effects and diminishing marginal utility. A change in the good's own price moves buyers along the curve; a change in tastes, income, the prices of substitutes or complements, expectations or the number of buyers shifts the whole curve. Market demand adds every buyer's quantity at each price.
